attempts.response: {"title":"3D Genome Analysis Identifies Enhancer Hijacking Mechanism for High-Risk Factors in Human T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia","authors":"Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang (Peking University Institute of Hematology); Leping Zhang (Peking University People's Hospital); Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu","field_subfield":"Computational/Bioinformatics Genomics (3D genome analysis of hematological malignancy)","type_of_paper":"Primary research: integrative multi-omics study (Hi-C, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq)","executive_summary":"This study integrates 3D genome architecture with transcriptomics to dissect the molecular etiology and prognosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). The authors analyzed 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy T-cell controls using RNA-seq, Hi-C, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq. They found that 3D genome organization at compartment, TAD, and loop levels, together with gene expression profiles, could hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T-cell differentiation trajectory. Approximately 29% of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with 3D genome alterations, and after accounting for transcription factor mediation, 3D genome alterations could associate with approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. The authors identified 46 translocations in 14/18 T-ALL samples, of which 34 were novel, and 44 new translocation-mediated loops. They demonstrated that translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusions could activate T-ALL-associated transcription factors, including ectopic HOXA cluster expression. Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression, but not other HOXA genes, was associated with immature phenotypes and poor outcomes. HOXA13 positivity was an independent predictor of overall survival in pediatric and young adult T-ALLs. The study suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk subgroup. The findings highlight the roles of 3D genome alterations in the etiology and prognosis of T-ALL. The transcriptome changes were highly consistent with 3D genome structural changes, supporting the use of RNA-seq as a biological readout for functional impact. The study also provided subtype-specific insights into ETP versus non-ETP ALL, and explained diverse HOXA expression patterns through 3D genome organizations. The results imply that 3D genome alterations may play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome and regulating T-ALL development. The newly identified translocations and enhancer hijacking mechanism may explain how T-ALL-associated transcription factors are ectopically activated and block differentiation at certain T-cell developmental stages. The study identified associations of ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression with poor survival, corresponding to a subtype currently incurable by standard treatments. summary.title: 3D Genome Analysis Identifies Enhancer Hijacking Mechanism for High-Risk Factors in Human T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
summary.authors: Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang (Peking University Institute of Hematology); Leping Zhang (Peking University People's Hospital); Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu
summary.field_subfield: Computational/Bioinformatics Genomics (3D genome analysis of hematological malignancy)
summary.type_of_paper: Primary research: integrative multi-omics study (Hi-C, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq)
summary.executive_summary: This study integrates 3D genome architecture with transcriptomics to dissect the molecular etiology and prognosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). The authors analyzed 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy T-cell controls using RNA-seq, Hi-C, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq. They found that 3D genome organization at compartment, TAD, and loop levels, together with gene expression profiles, could hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T-cell differentiation trajectory. Approximately 29% of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with 3D genome alterations, and after accounting for transcription factor mediation, 3D genome alterations could associate with approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. The authors identified 46 translocations in 14/18 T-ALL samples, of which 34 were novel, and 44 new translocation-mediated loops. They demonstrated that translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusions could activate T-ALL-associated transcription factors, including ectopic HOXA cluster expression. Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression, but not other HOXA genes, was associated with immature phenotypes and poor outcomes. HOXA13 positivity was an independent predictor of overall survival in pediatric and young adult T-ALLs. The study suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk subgroup. The findings highlight the roles of 3D genome alterations in the etiology and prognosis of T-ALL. The transcriptome changes were highly consistent with 3D genome structural changes, supporting the use of RNA-seq as a biological readout for functional impact. The study also provided subtype-specific insights into ETP versus non-ETP ALL, and explained diverse HOXA expression patterns through 3D genome organizations. The results imply that 3D genome alterations may play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome and regulating T-ALL development. The newly identified translocations and enhancer hijacking mechanism may explain how T-ALL-associated transcription factors are ectopically activated and block differentiation at certain T-cell developmental stages. The study identified associations of ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression with poor survival, corresponding to a subtype currently incurable by standard treatments. Overall, the work advances understanding of the 3D genome in leukemia and suggests potential therapeutic targets.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study integrates 3D genome architecture with transcriptomics to dissect the molecular etiology and prognosis of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). The authors analyzed 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy T-cell controls using RNA-seq, Hi-C, ChIP-seq, and ATAC-seq. They found that 3D genome organization at compartment, TAD, and loop levels, together with gene expression profiles, could hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T-cell differentiation trajectory. Approximately 29% of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with 3D genome alterations, and after accounting for transcription factor mediation, 3D genome alterations could associate with approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. The authors identified 46 translocations in 14/18 T-ALL samples, of which 34 were novel, and 44 new translocation-mediated loops. They demonstrated that translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusions could activate T-ALL-associated transcription factors, including ectopic HOXA cluster expression. Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression, but not other HOXA genes, was associated with immature phenotypes and poor outcomes. HOXA13 positivity was an independent predictor of overall survival in pediatric and young adult T-ALLs. The study suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk subgroup. The findings highlight the roles of 3D genome alterations in the etiology and prognosis of T-ALL. The transcriptome changes were highly consistent with 3D genome structural changes, supporting the use of RNA-seq as a biological readout for functional impact. The study also provided subtype-specific insights into ETP versus non-ETP ALL, and explained diverse HOXA expression patterns through 3D genome organizations. The results imply that 3D genome alterations may play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome and regulating T-ALL development. The newly identified translocations and enhancer hijacking mechanism may explain how T-ALL-associated transcription factors are ectopically activated and block differentiation at certain T-cell developmental stages. The study identified associations of ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression with poor survival, corresponding to a subtype currently incurable by standard treatments. Overall, the work advances understanding of the 3D genome in leukemia and suggests potential therapeutic targets.

Research Context
The 3D genome alterations play important roles in tumorigenesis, including hematological malignancies. How 3D genome alterations provide insights into T-ALL patients is largely unknown. 3D genome organization could hierarchically classify different subtypes of T-ALL. Translocations are major driving forces for tumorigenesis, especially for leukemia. HOXA-positive T-ALLs represent a homogeneous clinical entity has not been systematically studied. The impact of 3D genome alterations on gene expression in T-ALLs needs investigation. 3D genome alterations could link to the etiology of T-ALL development.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how 3D genome alterations provide insights into T-ALL patients. The hypothesis is that 3D genome organization could classify T-ALL subtypes by differentiation trajectory. The hypothesis is that 3D genome alterations associate with a large fraction of upregulated genes. The hypothesis is that translocations mediate enhancer hijacking and gene fusions activating transcription factors. The hypothesis is that ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is associated with poor outcomes. The hypothesis is that 3D genome alterations play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome. The hypothesis is that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit high-risk T-ALL patients. The hypothesis is that the transcriptome serves as a biological readout for 3D genome alterations. The hypothesis is that T-ALL chromosomal organizations represent frozen stages of T cell development. The hypothesis is that HOXA13 positivity is an independent predictor of overall survival.

Methodological Details
The study analyzed 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy T cell controls. Eighteen T-ALL patient samples were collected under the protocol approved by the ethics committee. ETP status was defined as previously published. Leukemia blast cells were prepared by density-gradient centrifugation of bone marrow samples. CD19-CD14-CD235-CD45+CD7+ cells were further purified by FACS analysis. Peripheral blood samples were obtained from four healthy donors. T cells were purified using the EasySep TM Direct Human T Cell Isolation Kit. RNA-seq libraries were prepared with TruSeq RNA Library Prep Kit v2. Paired-end RNA-seq reads were generated with an average depth of 15 million read pairs. Reads were aligned to the hg19 genome with TopHat (v2.1.0). DESeq2 was applied to identify DEGs with FDR <0.01 and fold change >2. Genes with fewer than 5 reads in 20% of the samples were excluded. ChIP-seq reads were mapped to the hg19 genome with Bowtie2 (v2.3.5). ATAC-seq reads were mapped with Bowtie2 using parameter -X 2000 --no-mixed --no-discordant --no-unal. Aligned reads were filtered for a minimum MAPQ of 20. Signal tracks and peaks were generated by using the -SPMR option in MACS2. FIMO was used to detect the 20 bp CTCF motif from the Homer motif database. Hi-C was performed on one million cells/sample, according to the BL-Hi-C protocol. Raw BL-Hi-C reads were processed by the in-house HiCpipe framework. ChIA-PET2 was used to trim the bridge linkers and HiC-Pro to align reads. Juicer was applied to generate individual or merged Hi-C files. Knight-Ruiz normalized matrices were used in the compartment and TAD analyses. The compartment was calculated with the eigenvector command of Juicer under 100 kb resolution. A or B compartments were defined by the over 70% sample majority rule. TAD boundaries were calculated by the Insulation score method with parameters -is 1000000 -ids 200000 -im mean -nt 0.1. Differential TAD boundaries were defined with a t-test FDR<0.01 and a difference higher than 50% quantile. A TAD was defined when its boundaries were detected in at least two conditions. The domain score was calculated by dividing the intra-TAD interactions with all interactions connected to the TAD. Differential domain scores were calculated with a t-test FDR<0.01 and fold change higher than 70% quantile. Loops were called by HiCCUPS. The differential loop detection method was adapted from Douglas et al. Loops were split into two distance ranges (> or < 150 kb) to minimize potential bias. Differential loops were called within each range (FDR < 0.1) and then combined. The loop anchors were analyzed by GREAT (v3.0.0) using the nearest gene within 100 kb. DAVID 6.8 was used for KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. hic_breakfinder was adapted to detect translocations in 18 T-ALL patient samples. The average depth of patient Hi-C samples is 486 million read pairs and the read length is 150 bp. Hi-C raw data were treated as single ends to refine the breakpoint locations to single base-pair resolution. The exact locations supported by more than 3 chimeric reads were identified as the actual breakpoints. A translocation was considered novel if any breakpoint was not near any known breakpoint within 100 kb. A gene near a breakpoint was considered upregulated if its FPKM was >1- and 2-fold higher than control samples. Hi-C heatmaps and Visual 4C plots were generated by MATLAB code.

Procedures And Architectures
The study integrated analyses of 3D genome alterations and differentially expressed genes. The 3D genome organization was analyzed at compartment, TAD, and loop levels. The gene expression profiles could hierarchically classify different subtypes of T-ALL. The PCA and hierarchical clustering showed transcriptome changes consistent with 3D genome structural changes. The T-ALL samples were projected onto the T cell developmental trajectory defined by RNA-seq analysis. The ETP ALL samples were arrested at the immature stage, corresponding to the LMPP to Thy1 stages. The non-ETP samples were arrested at the Thy2 to Thy4 stages. The ETP and non-ETP ALL samples showed 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops. The Pearson's correlation coefficient between gene expression changes and loop strength was 0.685. The genes associated with ETP enhanced loops were enriched in immune response-activating signal transduction. The genes associated with non-ETP enhanced loops were enriched in TCR V(D)J recombination. The RcisTarget was used to predict the key transcription factors controlling upregulated genes. The SOX4, WT1 and TFDP2 potentially regulated approximately 28% of the upregulated genes. The translocation-mediated loops were named and analyzed across the translocated chromosomes. The ends of the translocation-mediated loops tend to anchor at the pre-existing loop anchors and CTCF binding sites. Nearly 78% of the translocation-mediated loops with CTCF motifs were linked to convergently oriented CTCF motifs. The loops may be mediated by the loop extrusion mechanism. The non-ETP ALL was classified into the HOXA, TLX and TAL subtypes. The loop-based hierarchical clustering matched the T-ALL subtypes. The cis mechanism involved translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking in the ETP, TLX and TAL subtypes. The trans mechanism involves translocation-mediated gene fusions. The HOXA cluster contains 11 genes. The HOXA + T-ALLs were separated into the 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups. The 11 HOXA genes were partitioned between 2 TADs. The 6 enhancer regions were labeled E1 to E12. The ChIP-seq analysis indicated increased interactions may be correlated with gains in the H3K27ac histone mark. The breakpoints were located within the 5' TAD, upstream of the HOXA13 gene. The translocation partner breakpoints lie in the gene bodies of the BCL11B and CDK6 genes. The CTCF binding sites could insulate genes located in the 3' TAD from the influence of the hijacked enhancers. The multivariate analysis showed HOXA13+ status as an independent predictor for overall survival. The HOXA11-A13+ cases were characterized by DN and ETP phenotypes. The HOXA11-A13+ cases had a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations.

Key Results
The 3D genome organization could hierarchically classify different subtypes of T-ALL. The transcriptome changes were highly consistent with the corresponding 3D genome structural changes. Approximately 29% (996/3392) of the DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. The genes associated with B-to-A compartment switches were mostly upregulated. The genes associated with A-to-B compartment switches were mostly downregulated. The genes were enriched in pathways such as hematopoietic cell lineage, transcriptional misregulation in cancer and cell cycle. The genes were enriched in pathways such as cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and T cell receptor signaling. The 3D genome alterations could associate with approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. The 56% could be directly related to structural alterations. The CDK6 locus exhibited a strong intra-TAD interaction. The MYB, MYCN, BCL11A, SOX4 and WT1 had increased D-scores. The SOX4, WT1 and TFDP2 had structural alterations at all 3 levels. The 46 translocations were identified in 14/18 T-ALL samples. The 34 were novel events and 26 were interchromosomal events. The 47% were located in noncoding regions. The 66% were located in the stable A compartment. The 44 new loops were formed across the translocated chromosomes. The 78% of the translocation-mediated loops with CTCF motifs were linked to convergently oriented CTCF motifs. The 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops were identified in ETP. The Pearson's correlation coefficient was 0.685. The 28% of the upregulated genes were potentially regulated by SOX4, WT1 and TFDP2. The 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups were identified. The 11 HOXA genes were partitioned between 2 TADs. The 6 enhancer regions were labeled E1 to E12. The 5/7 HOXA+ samples had translocation-mediated fusion events. The HOXA11-A13+ cases had a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations. The HOXA13+ status was an independent predictor for overall survival. The TAL+ positivity was associated with better overall survival. The TLX positivity had no association with the outcome.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 3D genome alterations could link to the etiology of T-ALL development. The transcriptome changes could serve as a biological readout for the functional impact of 3D genome alterations. The chromosomal organizations of T-ALL may represent different frozen stages of T cell development. The translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking or fusion events may drive ectopic transcription factor activation. The hijacked enhancers are from genes normally expressed during T cell development. The ectopic expression blocks normal differentiation. The fusion proteins recruit histone methyltransferase DOT1L to the HOXA locus. The differential HOXA gene expressions were associated with different 3D genome organizations. The increased interactions may be correlated with gains in the H3K27ac histone mark. The translocations mediated new loop formations between the 5' of the HOXA cluster and active enhancers. The CTCF binding sites could insulate genes located in the 3' TAD from the influence of the hijacked enhancers. The 3D genome alterations may play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome. The 3D genome alterations may regulate T-ALL development. The ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is associated with poor survival. The anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this group of patients.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study relied on a small sample size of 18 T-ALL patients and 4 healthy controls. The study did not report the random seed, train/test split, or specific demographic details. The study did not report the demographics of the patients. The study did not report the specific statistical methods in detail.
